metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) prediction. Under the TTB theory, subjects process cues in descending order of validity and choose the option favored by the first discriminating cue. For this experimental design, TTB makes deterministic predictions on all trials. In contrast, Tallying counts overall feature wins. On trials 1-6, the Tallying prediction is diametrically opposed to TTB (yielding ~0% agreement), and on trials 7-8 Tallying guesses (~50% agreement). Thus, data simulated under TTB will yield a metric value near 1.0, while data simulated under Tallying will yield a value near 0.125, resulting in an enormous and highly reliable gap between the two theories.

This metric isolates the exact trials where Tallying and Take The Best make strictly opposite deterministic predictions (the 'opposition' trials in the design). It calculates the proportion of choices on these trials that align with the Tallying heuristic. Under the advocated Tallying theory, this proportion will be high (close to 1, subject to noise), whereas under the competing Take The Best theory, the proportion will be low (close to 0), ensuring maximum separation between the two theories.

By design, Option A is always favored by the first discriminating cue in all 8 trial types. Therefore, Take The Best (TTB) predicts a constant probability of choosing Option A across all trials, depending only on the subject's noise parameters. Consequently, the standard deviation of the proportion of A choices across the 8 trial types should be very small for TTB (reflecting only binomial sampling noise). In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model evaluates the weighted sum of all cues. Because the cue trade-offs and absolute value differences vary drastically across the 8 trial types, WADD predicts highly variable choice probabilities for Option A (e.g., very confident on some trials, near-guessing or even preferring B on others, depending on the gamma parameter). Thus, WADD will yield a significantly higher standard deviation of choice proportions across trial types.

In the chosen experimental design, Take The Best (TTB) consistently identifies Option A as the winner across all 8 trial types because the first discriminating cue always favors Option A. Consequently, TTB predicts a uniform probability of choosing Option A across all trials, leading to a near-zero true variance in choice probabilities across trial types. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy integrates all cues, meaning the number of opposing cues significantly modulates choice confidence. Thus, WADD predicts highly variable choice probabilities across the 8 trial types. By calculating the variance of each subject's mean response across the 8 unique trial pairs, this metric will yield a much higher value for data generated under WADD compared to TTB.

The Weighted Additive (WADD) theory predicts highly deterministic choices (probabilities near 0 or 1) because subjects consistently apply subjective weights to the cues, leading to strong preferences on most trials. The Random Guessing theory, conversely, predicts that choice proportions will hover closely around 0.5 due to high noise and lapse rates. By calculating the absolute deviation of each subject's choice proportion from 0.5 for each trial type and averaging them, we directly quantify the 'extremeness' of their choices. WADD will yield high values (close to 0.5), whereas Random Guessing will yield low values (driven mostly by finite-sample binomial variance, around 0.22 for 12 repetitions).

This metric calculates the mean absolute deviation of choice proportions from 0.5 for each unique trial type. The Random Guessing / High-Noise theory predicts that choice proportions will be very close to 0.5 on all trials, resulting in a low absolute deviation (driven purely by binomial noise over 12 repetitions, yielding ~0.22). The Advocated WADD theory predicts highly deterministic choices on many trial types, pushing choice proportions close to 0 or 1, resulting in a high absolute deviation (closer to 0.5). Averaging this across all trial types per subject provides a highly stable measure of choice determinism.
